title: Four kinds of devotees (7.13–7.19)
hook: people come to God in trouble, in curiosity, in need, and in knowing; the Gita calls all four noble

segments.voice: Yesterday: vijnana, one in a thousand, and the world strung like pearls on a thread. Your line was rare. Did you catch the thread in anything ordinary? Day one hundred eighty-four.

Walk into a temple on any evening and look at the faces. A mother whose son is in the hospital. A student the night before an exam. A man whose shop isn't doing well, asking for a better year. A teenager who's just curious what all this is. An old woman who's been coming every day for sixty years and doesn't seem to need anything at all. Some people might say only one of them is here for the right reason. The Gita, chapter seven, looks at the same crowd, and says something more generous.
screen: `A MOTHER. A STUDENT. A SHOPKEEPER.` → `A CURIOUS TEENAGER.` → `SIXTY YEARS OF EVENINGS.`

segments.voice: First, the problem. The world is bewildered by the three gunas, Krishna says, the three strands of nature, and so it doesn't see him beyond them. His power of illusion is hard to cross, but those who turn to him cross it. Then verse sixteen. Four kinds of good people turn to me, Arjuna. The arta: the one in distress. The jijnasu: the one who wants to know. The artharthi: the one who seeks something, wealth, security, a good outcome. And the jnani: the one who knows. That's the mother, the teenager, the shopkeeper, and the old woman. Here's what's striking. All four are called good people, and verse eighteen calls all of them noble: udara, generous, large-hearted. Nobody gets turned away for coming in trouble or coming with a request. But one stands out. The one who knows, verse seventeen says, always united, devoted to one alone, is the best. I am very dear to that one, and that one is dear to me. Verse eighteen goes further: the one who knows is my very self. And verse nineteen describes the journey there. At the end of many births, the one who knows takes refuge in me, seeing that Vasudeva is everything. Such a great soul, Krishna says, is very hard to find. So the ladder isn't a test you pass or fail. You can come in scared. You can come in curious. You can come asking for a job. The door is open. And the Gita keeps walking you toward the fourth. That's today's word: four kinds of devotees.
screen: `THE ONE IN DISTRESS.` · `THE ONE WHO WANTS TO KNOW.` · `THE ONE WHO SEEKS SOMETHING.` · `THE ONE WHO KNOWS.` · then, large: `ALL FOUR ARE NOBLE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and ask yourself honestly which of the four you are today. Are you here in some kind of trouble? Out of curiosity? Wanting something to change? Or just to be here? There's no wrong answer; the Gita calls all four noble. Breathe with whatever you found. Then, for the last part of the sit, let the reason go, and simply sit, as the one who doesn't need anything. The bell holds the time.
Jnani. The one who knows, the fourth and dearest of four kinds of devotees: the one in distress, the one who wants to know, the one who seeks something, and the one who knows. All four noble.
Your line: the one who knows. Today, notice why you reach for something bigger than you, and don't be embarrassed by the reason. Day one hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Hindu temples welcome people who come for every reason: prayers in illness or trouble, questions, requests for success or a good year, and daily worship with no request at all; Gita 7.16 is often cited to honor all of them.

fork.setup: four people come to worship: one in trouble, one curious, one asking for something, one who knows. which ones does verse 18 call noble?
fork.reveal: all four: udarah, noble. then Krishna says the one who knows is dearest, his very self.

original.note: Sanskrit: jnani, the one who knows; the fourth and dearest of the four kinds of devotees (7.16–18).

trapdoor: what you thought: real devotion doesn't ask for anything.
what it means: people come in trouble, curiosity, need or knowing, and all four are noble; the one who knows is dearest.

what a scholar hears: 7.16 names arta, jijnasu, artharthi and jnani; 7.19's 'vasudevah sarvam iti', Vasudeva is all, is read by nondualist commentators as oneness and by devotional ones as total dependence on the Lord.

notes: Artharthi is glossed as 'seeks something: wealth, security, a good outcome'; some translate 'seeker of wealth', others 'seeker of a goal'. Confirm.
7.15 (evildoers don't turn to him) is left out for length.
Scholar floor on how nondualist and devotional commentators read 7.19 is a simplification; confirm.
